summary: This document defines an RTCP Extended Report block for reporting a simple discard count metric, for use in a range of RTP applications.

eli5.summary: This is a count of packets thrown away on arrival, reported back to the sender.

questions: what is rtcp xr discard count
what is a discarded rtp packet
difference between lost and discarded packets
subtitle: A small RTCP report block that tells a sender how many packets arrived fine but were never played.

tldr.problem: Packets can arrive correctly yet be thrown away before playout, for example because they came too late, too early or as duplicates. Existing loss counters do not show this.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7002 defines an RTCP Extended Report block (block type 24) with a fixed 12-byte layout. It carries a 32-bit Discard Count and a 2-bit Discard Type that says why packets were discarded.
tldr.outcome: Senders and network managers can tell discard problems apart from loss and adjust transmission or diagnose user-experience problems. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 7002 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2013, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is meant to be used alongside RFC 7003.

sections.title: Counting Packets That Were Never Played
sections.content:
RFC 7002 adds a new block type to the RTCP Extended Report (XR) framework from RFC 3611. The block reports the number of packets that were received correctly but never played out, typically because they arrived too late (buffer underflow) or too early (buffer overflow).

The metric applies both to systems that repair lost packets, with forward error correction or retransmission, and to those that do not. It helps identify, and characterize the severity of, transport problems that may affect how users perceive a service delivered over RTP.

The block can be used together with the Burst/Gap Discard block from RFC 7003. Sent together, the two let a receiver of the reports calculate burst/gap summary statistics such as the gap discard rate. The block belongs to the class of transport-related end-system metrics defined in RFC 6792.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a mail truck brings your letter but you cannot use it because it came at the wrong time. This RFC lets the receiver tell the sender how many letters ended up unused.

sections.title: Received, Lost and Discarded
sections.content:
The RFC sorts every packet into exactly one of three classes. A packet is lost if it fails to arrive within an implementation-specific time window. A packet that arrives within that window but is too early or too late to be played out, or is thrown away before playout because of duplication or redundancy, is discarded. Everything else is received (or OK).

A packet that arrives in the window but is dropped later by a higher-layer decoder, for example because of a decoding error, is not counted as discarded. The discard count metric counts only discarded packets, so it complements the loss count in RFC 3550 and the post-repair loss metric in RFC 5725.
sections.eli5: A letter is either delivered and read, never shows up, or shows up but gets binned. Only the binned ones are counted here.

sections.title: Where and How It Is Measured
sections.content:
The measurement is made at the receiving end of the RTP stream and covers one stream, identified by its SSRC. The block does not carry its own timing. It relies on the separate Measurement Information Block from RFC 6776, which describes the measurement period in use.

Because of that, the block MUST be sent in the same compound RTCP packet as the Measurement Information Block. If a receiver gets the block without the measurement interval in the same compound packet, it MUST discard the block.

The number of packets expected in the period is not repeated in this block. It can be worked out from a pair of extended sequence numbers in the Measurement Information Block.
sections.eli5: The count only makes sense with a calendar saying which days it covers, so the count and the calendar must arrive in the same envelope.

sections.title: The Discard Count Metrics Block
sections.content:
The block is fixed-size. It starts with BT=24 in an 8-bit Block Type field, then the 2-bit Interval Metric flag (I), the 2-bit Discard Type (DT), 4 reserved bits and a 16-bit Block Length that MUST be 2. Next come the 32-bit SSRC of Source and the 32-bit Discard Count.

The I flag says what the count covers: I=10 is the most recent interval between reports, and I=11 is a cumulative total. The value I=01 (sampled) MUST NOT be sent because discards can only be measured over definite intervals, and I=00 is reserved. Receivers MUST discard blocks with either value.

The Discard Type is 00 for duplicates or packets thrown away before playout, 01 for too early and 10 for too late. DT=11 is reserved. An endpoint MAY report any combination of types by putting several blocks in one RTCP XR packet.

The Discard Count is an unsigned value. If it exceeds 0xFFFFFFFD, the value 0xFFFFFFFE MUST be reported as an over-range measurement, and 0xFFFFFFFF MUST be reported if the measurement is unavailable. Reserved bits MUST be zero when sent and ignored on receipt. A block with any Block Length other than 2 MUST be discarded.

Some systems send duplicate RTP packets for robustness. The RFC says this is NOT RECOMMENDED because it breaks RTCP packet statistics, and points to a stream duplication mechanism that does not.
sections.eli5: The block is a short form with a few tick boxes: whether the count is for the last stretch or the whole time, and why the packets were binned. The last line is the number itself.

sections.title: Signaling With SDP
sections.content:
Use of XR blocks can be announced in the Session Description Protocol through the rtcp-xr attribute from RFC 3611. This RFC adds one new xr-format value, pkt-discard-count, to signal this block.

In an offer/answer exchange, the existing rules for unilateral rtcp-xr parameters from RFC 3611 apply. Signaling is optional, since XR blocks MAY be used without prior signaling.
sections.eli5: Before a game you can tell the other team you will keep score of a new thing. You do not have to, but it is polite.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Very detailed error information, such as the over-range or unavailable values, could give an attacker insight into the security processing. Where that matters, the implementation should apply encryption and authentication to this block, for example by using the AVPF profile together with Secure RTP, as in the combined SAVPF profile of RFC 5124 and RFC 3711.

Apart from that, the RFC believes the block adds no new security considerations beyond those in RFC 3611. Because it carries no per-packet statistics, the confidentiality risk noted in RFC 3611 does not apply.
sections.eli5: If a report says too much, a snoop could learn how your system works, so secret reports should be sent in a locked box.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC assigns block type value 24 to the Discard Count Metrics Block in the IANA RTCP XR Block Type Registry. It also registers the new SDP parameter pkt-discard-count in the RTCP XR SDP Parameters Registry.

Appendix A restates the metric using the template from RFC 6390, mostly by pointing back to the sections above.
sections.eli5: The RFC puts its new block's name and number in the official phone book so nobody else uses them.

fields.name: I
fields.desc: Interval (10) or cumulative (11); 01 and 00 must not be sent.

fields.name: DT
fields.desc: Discard type: 00 duplicate, 01 too early, 10 too late.

fields.name: SSRC of Source
fields.desc: The stream the report is about.

fields.name: Discard Count
fields.desc: Packets discarded over the interval or cumulative period.
